newsitem.title: FRANCE: Frech govt ready to resume bank talks.
newsitem.headline: Frech govt ready to resume bank talks.

text.p: The French government said it was willing to restart talks with employees occupying the Paris headquarters of troubled bank Credit Foncier on Thursday, the seventh day of the sit-in, after they released its chairman.

Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure, taking an apparently more conciliatory stance, said mediator Philippe Rouvillois would make contact with unions fighting to stall a plan to break up the home loans bank.

"At 0830 (0730 GMT) the mediator appointed by the government will make contact with the unions and if there is a formula other than the one on the table at the moment, we are fully open to negotiation," Lamassoure told RTL radio.

"In the meantime, and this is very important, the draft law which was prepared by the government to save the business ... and avoid all straight layoffs at Credit Foncier is being kept in waiting," he said.
Talks were broken off after chairman Jerome Meyssonnier was held hostage during the ocupation. However, he was released on Wednesday.
An employee contacted inside the downtown headquarters said several hundred staff were still keeping vigil while union leaders met to discuss their next move, pending contact with Rouvillois.

Lamassoure reiterated the government's determination not to bail the bank out with taxpayers' money, but appeared to take a softer line by saying draft legislation concerning the break-up was being kept in waiting.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis unveiled plans in July for a partial takeover of the 145-year-old bank by the cooperatively run home loans group Credit Immobilier and to spin off the rest into a new holding company to be wound down in the coming years.

He argues that Credit Immobilier would secure the jobs of 1,500 staff and that another 800 would be kept working for the new state holding company. Plans to offer the rest of the 3,300 staff early retirement packages had been in the pipeline before the break-up plan was announced in the summer.

Employees have been occupying the building since Friday, taking turns preparing food and spending the night in the giant, marble-columned central hall in sleeping bags, but also keeping Credit Foncier branches around the country open for business.

Meyssonnier, who is desperately seeking alternatives, said after his release that talks would now be able to restart. These would aim to to find a better solution for the staff of a bank best known for providing cheap home loans to poorer families.
Amid record unemployment and intense media coverage, Arthuis has been under mounting pressure from opposition politicians and some from his own political camp to find another way out.
Credit Foncier has already been "nationalised" in the first stage of the break-up after losing 11 billion francs ($1.98 billion) in 1995.

But unions argue, with considerable political backing, that the accounts were overloaded to trigger the fall and Meyssonnier himself has predicted a profit of one billion francs this year. ($1=5.547 French Franc)
